# Getting the strongest protection from Shield

**This file is generated from `shield/protection.py`.** Edit the practices there,
not here — the same list drives `GET /shield/jobs/<id>/protection`, which tells you
which of these you are currently getting and which you are not.

---

## Why any of this matters

A Shield record has to survive being read by someone who wants it to fall apart —
an opposing contractor, an adjuster looking for a reason to deny, a lawyer paid to
find the gap. Every practice below exists because skipping it hands that reader
something to work with.

The first four cost seconds. They matter more than everything else combined.

---

## 1. Set the job site address and coordinates when you buy Shield.

**When:** at purchase &nbsp;·&nbsp; **Who:** the homeowner

**Why it works.** It is the only geographic reference the contractor cannot move. Every later photo is measured against it.

**What it costs you to skip.** There is nothing to geofence against. A photo taken in another city passes every location check.

---

## 2. Generate and lock the checkpoint schedule before the contractor begins.

**When:** before work starts &nbsp;·&nbsp; **Who:** the homeowner

**Why it works.** Requirements fixed in advance cannot have been chosen to fit the photographs. This is the strongest structural property of the record, and it costs nothing.

**What it costs you to skip.** An opposing party will argue the criteria were written around the evidence. It is a difficult argument to answer.

---

## 3. Take the photo while the work is in front of you, not from memory at the end of the day.

**When:** at each checkpoint &nbsp;·&nbsp; **Who:** the contractor

**Why it works.** The capture time in the file is what the solar check and the note window are both measured from.

**What it costs you to skip.** Shadow geometry stops corroborating, and every note is pushed into a weaker hearsay exception.

---

## 4. Write the note within five minutes of the photo.

**When:** at each checkpoint &nbsp;·&nbsp; **Who:** the contractor

**Why it works.** FRE 803(1) — a present sense impression is admissible without the writer testifying, because contemporaneity is what makes deliberate misrepresentation unlikely.

**What it costs you to skip.** After roughly half an hour you are relying on recorded recollection or the business-records rule instead, both of which need you available and credible.

---

## 5. Record what you saw and measured. Leave conclusions out.

**When:** at each checkpoint &nbsp;·&nbsp; **Who:** the contractor

**Why it works.** 803(1) covers descriptions and explanations, not opinions — so a conclusion is inadmissible under it and uncheckable by a reader.

**What it costs you to skip.** "Looks good, all to code" carries no weight and invites the question of what you actually observed.

---

## 6. Photograph and annotate every checkpoint, including the boring ones.

**When:** throughout &nbsp;·&nbsp; **Who:** the contractor

**Why it works.** FRE 803(6) requires that making the record was a regular practice. Consistency is the qualification.

**What it costs you to skip.** Gaps are the first thing an opposing expert points at, and a partial record invites the inference that the missing ones were unfavourable.

---

## 7. Export the evidence package and keep the chain head hash somewhere outside this service — an email to yourself is enough.

**When:** periodically, and at close-out &nbsp;·&nbsp; **Who:** the homeowner

**Why it works.** A head hash you held last month proves the history you were shown has not been rewritten since, including by us.

**What it costs you to skip.** You are trusting the operator's copy of the record. That is precisely the assumption a dispute will test.

---

## 8. Correct a note by amending it, and say why.

**When:** when you get something wrong &nbsp;·&nbsp; **Who:** the contractor

**Why it works.** A visible correction reads as careful. Notes here cannot be edited, so this is the only route — and it is the better one.

**What it costs you to skip.** Nothing: the system will not let you rewrite. But asking for an edit signals a misunderstanding worth correcting.

---

## The two-minute version

**Homeowner, before work starts:**

1. Set the site address and coordinates when you buy.
2. Generate and lock the checkpoint schedule — *before* the contractor begins.
3. Tell the contractor the notes are part of what you paid for.

**Contractor, at every checkpoint:**

4. Photograph it while you are standing there.
5. Write the note within five minutes.
6. Write what you measured, not what you concluded.
7. Do it on the boring checkpoints too.

**Homeowner, periodically and at close-out:**

8. Export the evidence package. Email yourself the chain head hash.

---

## The one nobody thinks of

Practice 7 — exporting the package and keeping the chain head hash somewhere
outside this service — is the only practice that protects you against *us*.

Everything else in Shield assumes the operator is honest. The hash chain makes
tampering detectable, but only if someone holds an earlier head to compare
against. If you hold a head hash from three months ago and the record still
verifies against it today, you know nothing was rewritten in between — by the
contractor, by a database administrator, or by TradeDeck.

An email to yourself is enough. It costs nothing and it is the difference between
trusting a record and being able to check one.

---

## What Shield still cannot do for you

Stated plainly so you are not surprised by it in a dispute:

- **It cannot prove a photo came off a camera sensor** rather than a file picker.
  The geofence and the solar check make a fabrication harder and more likely to
  be caught, but only capture-time attestation in a native app would close this.
- **It cannot make anything admissible.** A judge decides that. What the export
  gives you is the foundation a lawyer needs to make the argument.
- **The AI assessment is an opinion, not a finding.** It is stated with its model
  and confidence, and the certification says explicitly that it is not a finding
  of code compliance.

None of that weakens the record. Overstating it would.
